title: C# built-in type aliases and characteristics
concepts: Most C# built-in type keywords alias named types; dynamic, delegate, and void have distinct semantics
Value types store values while reference types store object references
Numeric types differ in range, precision, representation, and platform dependence; decimal is not IEEE binary floating point
The built-in type set includes numeric, Boolean, character, object, string, dynamic, delegate, and void forms
Choosing a type means balancing domain meaning, range, precision, interoperability, and API expectations

items: Native-sized integers are represented as System.IntPtr/System.UIntPtr and have 32-bit or 64-bit width according to process architecture; C# 9 introduced native integer language support and operators/conversions. They are not managed object references.

sourceSnapshot.authority: Microsoft Learn C# built-in type reference and C# language specification

scopeExclusions: Numeric literal syntax and numeric conversion rules, covered in a separate topic
Nullable forms such as T? and nullable reference annotations, covered separately
Framework types not exposed as C# built-in keywords
Formatting and parsing APIs for values
accuracyFacts: Most keywords are aliases, but dynamic is represented as object with runtime binding behavior, delegate declares custom delegate types, and void represents absence of a type.

Value-type variables contain instances and reference-type variables contain references; do not claim the language requires local values on the stack, objects elsewhere, or references to be physical addresses.
decimal uses finite-precision base-10 representation and many decimal fractions are exact, but arithmetic may round; no blanket speed claim.
float and double use IEEE 754 binary32/binary64 and support NaN/infinities; decimal is a 96-bit integer scaled by a power of ten, occupies 16 bytes, and has no NaN/infinities.
char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, not necessarily one complete Unicode scalar; supplementary scalars use surrogate pairs.
string is immutable, stores UTF-16 code units, and its equality operators compare string contents.
nint/nuint width follows process architecture; they are not managed object references and do not automatically make pointer arithmetic safe.
object is the root base type with ref-struct restrictions; converting value types to object boxes, while dynamic binding can fail at runtime.
Integral constant conversions, runtime conversions, and arithmetic overflow follow distinct rules; distinguish compile-time constants and checked/unchecked runtime contexts.
